episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, August seventh, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.
<break time="1.0s"/>
The top story this week comes from Inside Higher Ed. At least a dozen universities have disabled Turnitin’s A.I.-detection software as institutions respond to evidence that detection tools can misidentify human writing. Yale, Vanderbilt, Johns Hopkins and Indiana have adopted policies that ban or discourage using detector results as the sole evidence of cheating. Northwestern, Georgetown and New York University are among the institutions that have turned off Turnitin’s detector.

The change comes as faculty continue to encounter A.I.-related academic-integrity cases. A national survey cited by Inside Higher Ed found that 73 percent of faculty had personally handled one. Studies of detection programs have also documented inconsistent results, false positives and bias against non-native English writers. Yale teaching-center leaders said programs that make generated prose sound more human can reduce or eliminate detection, creating a continuing contest between detection and evasion tools.

Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business now directs faculty toward assignments focused on process, reasoning and authentic engagement. Kevin Yee of the University of Central Florida said traditional assessments may remain workable in in-person courses with fewer than 30 students. Larger classes may require redesigned work, blue-book exams or oral exams. A guide he co-authored offers dozens of ideas, including asking students to document how they used A.I. Marc Watkins of the University of Mississippi said scaling approaches such as oral exams will require labor, resources and institutional support.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Turning to Case Study coverage, Miami University is building discipline-specific A.I. competencies into majors across 49 academic departments, the university reports. The faculty-led A.I. in the Majors initiative begins during the twenty twenty-six to twenty twenty-seven academic year. The first cohort includes 13 volunteer departments and an estimated forty-nine hundred students. A second cohort of 15 departments is scheduled to begin work in twenty twenty-seven, followed by 21 departments during the twenty twenty-seven to twenty twenty-eight academic year.

Each department in the first group has selected one major for the initial curriculum work. Speech Pathology and Audiology offers an early example. Its working group spent more than a year developing competencies that move through academic, research and clinical courses. Introductory students will learn foundational A.I. awareness. Seniors in clinical practica will address application and accountability when using A.I. to document patient treatment. Miami also offers an A.I. bachelor’s degree and a free, self-paced five-module fundamentals program for students, faculty and staff.
<break time="1.0s"/>
From Insights and Trends, employer questions about student A.I. skills are rising. A student-led Kogod School of Business report covered by Poets and Quants found that the share of students who encountered those questions increased from 11.6 percent in twenty twenty-four to 42.6 percent in twenty twenty-six. The analysis included 483 undergraduate and graduate responses gathered across three years.

More than 80 percent of respondents had used A.I. for academic work during the previous six months. The share reporting at least 11 uses per week rose from 6.2 percent to 29 percent, while the share reporting no weekly use fell by nearly three-quarters. Requests for coding and technical instruction also increased, from 3.6 percent of qualitative responses in twenty twenty-five to 19.8 percent in twenty twenty-six. Nearly half raised academic-integrity concerns. Career-related worries rose from 13.4 percent to 20.2 percent, and about 44 percent reported using A.I. as a shortcut or substitute at some point.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Meanwhile, at Boston University, a student-built classroom-assignment model reduced average wasted seats by roughly 92 percent while processing about forty-five hundred courses. Boston University reports that Joey Russoniello, a twenty twenty-six graduate of the Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, developed the project with Information Services and Technology through the university’s clinic program.

The web application accepts course and room data, then analyzes enrollment, capacity and geography while preventing double bookings. Russoniello translated the scheduling problem into a mathematical optimization model with hundreds of constraints. An early version took about nine hours to find a solution. The final version completed the work in about 90 seconds.

The model also reduced the average distance between a course’s home department and assigned classroom from 0.15 miles to 0.05 miles. The project’s code is publicly available. Boston University’s Information Services and Technology unit and Registrar’s Office are reviewing the tool, and the clinic project is continuing with new students.
<break time="1.0s"/>
From the research front, a West Virginia University study tested whether a generative A.I. model could produce realistic psychiatry training cases. WDTV reports that the study, published in the journal N.P.J. Digital Medicine, created fictional vignettes involving people with mental-health conditions who were also using A.I. chatbots.

The cases covered schizophrenia, anxiety, mood disorders and major depression. Reviewers gave the generated material high marks for clear language, symptom accuracy and educational value. The study also identified limits requiring human oversight. In severe-depression scenarios, the researchers said training cases include an assessment of suicidal thinking, but the model did not reliably identify and prioritize that concern on its own. They also warned that a chatbot’s tendency to agree with users could validate delusions in some psychiatric scenarios.

The researchers described potential for the cases when paired with faculty supervision, structured discussion and safety guidelines. They said more study is needed before broader use in mental-health professional training.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Turning to Practical Tips, six reusable prompts can convert existing course materials into accessibility supports. An Inside Higher Ed essay by Merrimack College professor Kathryn Welby describes prompts for checklists, roadmaps, guided notes, graphic organizers, plain-language assignment directions and draft analytic rubrics.

One prompt asks a generative A.I. tool to convert a full syllabus into a week-by-week printable checklist with every due date and student-friendly language. Another requests a one-page course roadmap showing modules, assignments, exams and deadlines. Faculty can also provide learning objectives and request guided notes with section headings, fill-in-the-blank prompts, key terms and a closing question. The essay describes each generated support as a first draft for faculty review.

Welby also reports evidence from 18 students in her doctoral qualitative research methods course. Across three assignment types, about 67 percent used an optional A.I.-generated graphic organizer as provided, and 28 percent adapted it. Students who followed the organizer closely averaged five to 13 points higher than students who did not use it.
<break time="1.0s"/>
In another Insights and Trends story, California is piloting a free A.I.-literacy microcredential. The Long Beach Press-Telegram reports that A.I.-Ready California enrolled 500 participants from the San Diego Community College District and a city reemployment program. About 250 participants had accessed the online curriculum as of July thirty-first.

The beginner-level program focuses on literacy rather than technical expertise. Its modules explain what A.I. is and how it works, examine limits and risks involving bias, ethics and sensitive information, and cover workplace and civic uses. Participants who complete the material earn a microcredential.

The partnership includes the California State University A.I. Workforce Acceleration Board, San Diego State University, state labor and innovation offices, the California Community Colleges and private organizations. Organizers plan to use pilot data before opening the program to all Californians, but the report did not give a statewide launch date. San Diego State has conducted annual surveys on A.I. needs since twenty twenty-three, and the university system and its partners have gathered more than one hundred thousand responses.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Finally, in Case Study coverage, Metropolitan State University of Denver is integrating A.I. instruction across business, journalism, engineering and teacher-preparation coursework. The university’s RED publication reports that business students can study A.I. through courses and certificates. Journalism students examine generative media production. Engineering students use A.I. in remote-sensing coursework, while future educators develop literacy through educational-technology classes.

Industrial Design student William Block used A.I.-powered tools to move a watch design from a sketch to a realistic rendering. He said the experience changed how he views his future role, with greater emphasis on managing A.I. output through discretion and careful evaluation.

The university is also adding A.I. Fundamentals, an elective open to every major, this fall. The course requires no programming experience and uses hands-on activities and case studies to cover machine learning, generative A.I., ethics, bias, privacy and decision-making. RED also cited workforce data showing that 88 percent of organizations use A.I. in at least one business function. Strada Education Foundation found that senior talent leaders were nearly three times more likely to expect A.I. to increase entry-level hiring than reduce it. More than 40 percent reported that A.I. had shifted new employees from routine administrative work toward analytical tasks.
<break time="1.0s"/>
That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Universities Replace A.I. Detectors With Redesigned Assessments

Yale, Vanderbilt, Johns Hopkins and Indiana have adopted policies that ban or discourage using detector results as the sole evidence of cheating, while Northwestern, Georgetown and New York University are among the institutions that have turned off Turnitin’s detector.

quickHits.headline: Miami Builds Discipline-Specific A.I. Into Every Department
quickHits.summary:
Forty-nine academic departments will build field-specific A.I. competencies into their majors through a staged initiative at Miami University, the university reported. The faculty-led A.I. in the Majors program begins during the 2026–27 academic year with 13 volunteer departments serving an estimated 4,925 students. A second cohort of 15 departments is scheduled to begin work in spring or fall 2027, followed by 21 departments during 2027–28.

Each department in the first cohort will select one major for the initial curriculum work. Speech Pathology and Audiology provides one example of how the model is intended to operate: its working group spent more than a year developing competencies that move through academic, research and clinical courses. Introductory communication-disorders students will learn foundational A.I. awareness, while seniors in clinical practica will address application and accountability when using A.I. to document patient treatment.

The initiative grew from the university’s MiamiTHRIVE strategic plan and is designed around each discipline rather than a single campuswide course. Miami also offers an A.I. bachelor’s degree and a free, self-paced five-module A.I. Fundamentals program for students, faculty and staff.

quickHits.headline: Employer Questions About Student A.I. Skills Rise
quickHits.summary:

The share reporting at least 11 uses per week increased from 6.2 percent to 29 percent, while the share reporting no weekly use fell by nearly three-quarters.

About 44 percent said they had used A.I. as a shortcut or substitute at some point. Kogod embeds A.I. work across its courses, including coding, data analysis and financial modeling.

quickHits.headline: Boston University Student Cuts Classroom Assignment Waste
quickHits.summary:
A classroom-assignment model reduced average wasted seats by roughly 92 percent while processing about 4,500 courses, Boston University reports. Joey Russoniello, a 2026 graduate of the Faculty of Computing & Data Sciences, developed the project with Information Services & Technology through the university’s clinic program during the 2025–26 academic year.

The project’s code is publicly available on GitHub. Boston University’s Information Services & Technology unit and Registrar’s Office are reviewing the tool, and the clinic project is continuing with new students.

quickHits.headline: WVU Tests ChatGPT for Psychiatry Training Cases
quickHits.summary:
ChatGPT-5 Pro generated realistic psychiatric training cases but did not reliably prioritize every safety concern, a West Virginia University study reported by WDTV found. Published in npj Digital Medicine, the study tested fictional vignettes involving people with mental-health conditions who were also using A.I. chatbots.

The cases covered schizophrenia, anxiety, mood disorders and major depression. The study also identified limits that require human oversight.

In severe-depression scenarios, the researchers said training cases need to prompt learners to assess suicidal thinking, yet the model could not be trusted to identify and prioritize that concern on its own. The researchers also warned that a chatbot’s tendency to agree with users could validate delusions in some psychiatric scenarios.

The findings support using generated cases with faculty supervision, structured discussion and safety guidelines rather than as an independent teaching system. The researchers said more study is needed before broader use in mental-health professional training.

quickHits.headline: Six A.I. Prompts Turn Course Materials Into Supports
quickHits.summary:
Six reusable prompts can turn existing course materials into accessibility supports such as checklists, roadmaps and guided notes, an Inside Higher Ed essay by Merrimack College professor Kathryn Welby explains. Each prompt assigns the model a role, supplies a specific course artifact and defines the required output.

One example asks an A.I. tool to convert a full syllabus into a week-by-week printable checklist with every due date and student-friendly language. Welby also reports classroom evidence from 18 students in her doctoral qualitative research methods course. Across three assignment types, about 67 percent used an optional A.I.-generated graphic organizer as provided and 28 percent adapted it. Students who followed the organizer closely averaged five to 13 points higher than students who did not use it, while the highest-scoring students extended beyond the provided structure.
